en.title: Civil Engineering: the whole course
en.short: What civil engineering covers, how BEng and HND courses are organised, and how to study them well.

sections.heading: What civil engineering is
sections.text:
Civil engineering is the planning, design, construction and maintenance of the works that a society shares. These include buildings, bridges, roads, railways, dams, water supply networks, drains and waste treatment plants. Most of these works are built only once, on a particular site, and they must serve the public safely for decades.

The subject matters because a failure can kill people and waste large public budgets. A good engineer therefore combines mathematics and science with judgement about uncertain loads, variable soils and limited money.

These summaries teach principles. They don’t replace a design code or a qualified engineer. Real designs must follow the current code and law of the country concerned, and a registered engineer must check and take responsibility for them. Codes differ by country and change over time. British Standards such as BS 8110 are still widely taught in Nigeria and Ghana, while Eurocodes replaced them in the UK, and a second generation of Eurocodes is due by 2028. Other countries use other documents. All numerical examples here are for learning only.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text:
A Nigerian BEng usually takes five years, including a period of industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Polytechnic students usually take an ND, then a period of supervised industrial work, then an HND. In most of the UK a BEng usually takes three years and an MEng four, while in Scotland each usually takes a year longer. Ghana and Kenya have their own patterns of degrees and diplomas.

The early years are shared with other engineering students: mathematics, mechanics, drawing and basic science. Later years move into civil engineering subjects with design classes, laboratory work and fieldwork. Most courses end with an individual project. A master’s degree adds advanced analysis and a research dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
First come engineering mathematics, statics and dynamics, strength of materials, construction materials, surveying and basic fluid mechanics. These give the tools for everything that follows.

Next comes structural analysis, which finds the internal forces in beams, trusses and frames. Reinforced concrete and steel design then use those forces to size real members.

Engineering geology describes the rocks and ground conditions of a site. Soil mechanics explains how the ground carries load, and it leads to foundation design. Hydraulics, hydrology and water supply deal with the movement and treatment of water. Environmental engineering covers wastewater, pollution and impact assessment.

Highway and transport engineering covers road geometry, pavements and traffic. Construction management covers planning, cost and contracts. Professional practice covers ethics, safety and registration, including COREN in Nigeria.

At master’s level, students study matrix methods, non-linear and dynamic analysis, finite element methods and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Solve problems by hand, and solve many of them. Reading a worked solution is not the same as being able to produce one. Draw a clear diagram before you write any equation. For structures, draw a free-body diagram. For soils, draw the layers and the water table. For water, draw the flow path and the datum.

Write the units on every line. Then ask whether the answer is reasonable. Do you expect a beam to deflect by 8 mm or by 800 mm? Learn typical values such as the unit weight of concrete and the yield strength of steel, so that you can notice errors.

Use software after you understand the hand method, and always check its results with a simple calculation. Take site visits and industrial training seriously, because they show how drawings become real works.

sections.heading: Common mistakes

keyPoints: Civil engineering covers structures, ground, water, transport, environment and construction.
These summaries teach principles and don’t replace a design code or a qualified engineer.
Design codes differ by country and change over time, so check the current one.
Draw a diagram, write units on every line, and check that answers are reasonable.
Understand the hand method before you trust software.

en.title: Engineering mathematics for civil engineers
en.short: The calculus, matrices, differential equations and statistics that civil engineering relies on.

sections.heading: Why the mathematics matters
sections.text:
Civil engineering uses mathematics to describe how loads, water and soil behave. Four tools appear again and again.

Calculus links quantities that change along a member. Load, shear force and bending moment are connected by differentiation and integration. Integration also gives areas, centroids and total forces.

Matrices organise many equations at once. A building frame analysed by computer may produce thousands of simultaneous equations.

Differential equations describe change. The bending of a beam, the vibration of a structure and the consolidation of clay are all governed by them.

Statistics deals with variation. Concrete strength, rainfall and traffic all vary, so design values are chosen using probability.

sections.heading: Worked example: total force from a varying load
sections.text:
A beam carries a load that grows along its length: w(x) = 6x kN/m, from x = 0 to x = 4 m. Find the total load and where it acts.

Total load = ∫ 6x dx from 0 to 4 = [3x²] = 3 × 16 = 48 kN
Moment about x = 0 = ∫ 6x² dx from 0 to 4 = [2x³] = 2 × 64 = 128 kN·m
Position of the resultant = 128 ÷ 48 = 2.67 m

Check: the resultant of a triangular load acts two-thirds of the way along, and 2/3 × 4 = 2.67 m.

sections.heading: Worked example: two equations by Cramer’s rule
sections.text:
Equilibrium gives two equations in the forces F₁ and F₂:
2F₁ + F₂ = 10
F₁ + 3F₂ = 15

The determinant of the coefficient matrix is D = (2 × 3) − (1 × 1) = 5.
F₁ = [(10 × 3) − (1 × 15)] ÷ 5 = 15 ÷ 5 = 3
F₂ = [(2 × 15) − (1 × 10)] ÷ 5 = 20 ÷ 5 = 4

Check: 2(3) + 4 = 10 and 3 + 3(4) = 15. Both are correct.

When a determinant is zero, the equations have no unique solution. In a structure, this can signal a mechanism.

keyPoints: Calculus links load, shear force, bending moment and deflection.
Matrices handle the large equation systems used in structural software.
Differential equations govern beam bending, vibration and consolidation.
A zero determinant means no unique solution, which can indicate a mechanism.
Statistics is needed because materials, rainfall and traffic all vary.

en.title: Statics: forces, moments and equilibrium
en.short: How to resolve forces, take moments and find the support reactions of a beam.

sections.heading: Forces and moments
sections.text:
Statics studies bodies that stay at rest. A force is a push or pull with a size and a direction, measured in newtons (N). A force can be resolved into two perpendicular components: a force F at angle θ to the horizontal has components F cos θ and F sin θ.

A moment is the turning effect of a force about a point. Its size is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action. Moments are measured in N·m or kN·m.

sections.heading: Equilibrium and supports
sections.text:
A body in a plane is in equilibrium when three conditions all hold:
ΣFx = 0 (horizontal forces balance)
ΣFy = 0 (vertical forces balance)
ΣM = 0 (moments about any point balance)

The first step is always a free-body diagram. This is a sketch of the body alone, with every load and every support reaction shown.

Supports are idealised. A roller gives one reaction, perpendicular to the surface. A pin gives two reactions, one horizontal and one vertical. A fixed support gives two reactions and a moment.

sections.heading: Worked example: beam reactions
sections.text:
A simply supported beam AB spans 6 m. It carries a 30 kN point load 2 m from A, and a uniform load of 5 kN/m over the whole span. Find the reactions RA and RB.

The uniform load totals 5 × 6 = 30 kN and acts at mid-span, 3 m from A.

Take moments about A:
6 × RB = (30 × 2) + (30 × 3) = 60 + 90 = 150
RB = 25 kN

Resolve vertically:
RA + RB = 30 + 30 = 60
RA = 60 − 25 = 35 kN

Check with moments about B:
6 × RA = (30 × 4) + (30 × 3) = 120 + 90 = 210
RA = 35 kN, which agrees.

Three reactions and three equations make this beam statically determinate.

keyPoints: In a plane, equilibrium means ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0.
Moment = force × perpendicular distance.
A roller gives 1 reaction, a pin gives 2, and a fixed support gives 3.
Always start with a free-body diagram.
Check reactions by taking moments about a second point.

en.title: Dynamics and basic vibration
en.short: Motion, Newton’s second law, energy, and the natural frequency of a simple structure.

sections.heading: Motion and force
sections.text:
Dynamics studies bodies that accelerate. Kinematics describes the motion alone. For constant acceleration a, with initial speed u and final speed v over distance s and time t:
v = u + at
s = ut + ½at²
v² = u² + 2as

Kinetics connects motion to force through Newton’s second law, F = ma.

The net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy, ½mv². The impulse on a body (force × time) equals its change in momentum, mv.

sections.heading: Worked example: a braking vehicle
sections.text:
A car of mass 1,500 kg travels at 72 km/h on a road near Nairobi. It brakes at a constant 5 m/s². Find the stopping distance, the stopping time and the braking force.

Speed: 72 ÷ 3.6 = 20 m/s
Distance: from 0 = 20² − 2(5)s, s = 400 ÷ 10 = 40 m
Time: t = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 s
Force: F = 1,500 × 5 = 7,500 N = 7.5 kN

Check by energy: ½ × 1,500 × 20² = 300,000 J. Work done by braking is 7,500 × 40 = 300,000 J. They agree.

Stopping distance grows with the square of speed.

sections.heading: Natural frequency of a simple structure
sections.text:
A structure that is disturbed will vibrate at its natural frequency. A simple model, with a single degree of freedom, is a mass m on a spring of stiffness k.

ω = √(k ÷ m), f = ω ÷ 2π, T = 1 ÷ f

Here ω is the angular frequency in rad/s, f is the frequency in Hz and T is the period in seconds.

Example: a water tank of mass 20,000 kg stands on a frame with sideways stiffness 2.0 × 10⁶ N/m.
ω = √(2.0 × 10⁶ ÷ 20,000) = √100 = 10 rad/s
f = 10 ÷ (2π) = 1.59 Hz
T = 1 ÷ 1.59 = 0.63 s

Resonance occurs when a repeating load has a frequency close to the natural frequency.

keyPoints: Newton’s second law is F = ma.
Kinetic energy is ½mv², so stopping distance grows with the square of speed.
Natural frequency is f = √(k ÷ m) ÷ 2π.
Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6.
Resonance occurs when a repeating load is close to the natural frequency.

en.title: Stress, strain and axial loading
en.short: Direct stress and strain, Hooke’s law, elastic modulus, thermal effects and factors of safety.

sections.heading: Stress and strain
sections.text:
Direct stress is force per unit area: σ = P ÷ A. Its unit is N/mm² (1 N/mm² = 1 MPa). Direct strain is the change in length per unit length: ε = δ ÷ L. Strain has no units.

For many materials at low stress, the two are proportional. This is Hooke’s law: σ = Eε. The constant E is Young’s modulus, also called the elastic modulus. It measures stiffness. Steel has E of about 200,000 N/mm², and normal concrete has about 30,000 N/mm².

Combining these gives the extension of a bar: δ = PL ÷ (AE).

A bar in tension also gets thinner. The ratio of sideways strain to lengthwise strain is Poisson’s ratio, about 0.3 for steel and about 0.2 for concrete.

sections.heading: The tensile test
sections.text:
A tensile test on mild steel shows a straight elastic line, then a yield point at about 250 N/mm², then strain hardening, and finally necking and fracture. Unloaded before yield, steel returns to its original length. After yield, a permanent plastic strain remains.

Brittle materials such as concrete fail with little warning. Ductile materials such as steel stretch a lot first, which gives warning.

sections.heading: Worked example: steel rod
sections.text:
A steel rod has diameter 20 mm and length 2 m. It carries a tension of 50 kN, and E = 200,000 N/mm².

A = π × 20² ÷ 4 = 314.2 mm²
σ = 50,000 ÷ 314.2 = 159.2 N/mm²
ε = 159.2 ÷ 200,000 = 0.000796
δ = 0.000796 × 2,000 = 1.59 mm

sections.heading: Temperature and safety
sections.text:
A temperature change ΔT produces a free strain αΔT. For steel, α is about 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C. If the bar cannot move, a stress develops: σ = EαΔT. For a 30 °C rise, σ = 200,000 × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 30 = 72 N/mm².

A factor of safety is the ratio of failure stress to allowable stress. Modern limit state codes use separate partial factors on loads and materials instead.

keyPoints: Stress σ = P ÷ A, strain ε = δ ÷ L, and σ = Eε in the elastic range.
Extension of a bar is δ = PL ÷ (AE).
1 N/mm² = 1 MPa.
E is about 200,000 N/mm² for steel and about 30,000 N/mm² for concrete.
Restrained thermal stress is σ = EαΔT.

en.title: Construction materials: concrete, steel, timber and masonry
en.short: Properties and testing of cement, aggregates, concrete, steel, timber, blocks and bitumen.

sections.heading: Cement and concrete
sections.text:
Concrete is a mixture of cement, water, fine aggregate (sand) and coarse aggregate (stone). Portland cement is made by burning limestone and clay, then grinding the product with a little gypsum. Cement reacts chemically with water in a process called hydration. Concrete hardens through this reaction, not through drying. For this reason it must be kept moist during curing.

The water-cement ratio is the main control on strength. Less water gives stronger and less permeable concrete, but the mix becomes harder to place. Admixtures can improve workability without adding water.

The slump test measures the workability of fresh concrete. The cube test measures strength, normally at 28 days. Some countries, and Eurocode 2, specify strength from cylinders as well as cubes, so a C25/30 concrete has a cylinder strength of 25 and a cube strength of 30 N/mm².

sections.heading: Worked example: batching and testing
sections.text:
A nominal 1:2:4 mix by mass has a water-cement ratio of 0.5. Assume a fresh density of 2,400 kg/m³.
Total parts = 1 + 2 + 4 + 0.5 = 7.5
Cement = 2,400 ÷ 7.5 = 320 kg/m³, or 6.4 bags of 50 kg
Sand = 640 kg/m³, stone = 1,280 kg/m³, water = 160 kg/m³
Check: 320 + 640 + 1,280 + 160 = 2,400 kg/m³

A 150 mm cube fails at 675 kN:
Strength = 675,000 ÷ (150 × 150) = 30 N/mm²

sections.heading: Other materials
sections.text:
Steel for reinforcement comes in mild and high-yield grades, commonly with yield strengths near 250 and 460 to 500 N/mm². Structural steel grades include S275 and S355. Steel is strong in tension and compression, but it must be protected from corrosion and fire.

Timber is light and renewable. Its strength depends on species, moisture content and the direction of the grain.

Masonry uses bricks, stone or blocks. Sandcrete blocks are common in Nigeria and Ghana. Their quality varies a lot, so testing matters.

Bitumen binds the aggregate in road surfacing. Its stiffness changes with temperature.

keyPoints: Concrete hardens by hydration, so it must be cured and kept moist.
A lower water-cement ratio gives stronger, less permeable concrete.
The slump test measures workability, and the cube test measures strength.
Cube and cylinder strengths differ, so check which one a code uses.
Steel is ductile but needs protection from corrosion and fire.

en.title: Surveying: principles and levelling
en.short: How to measure heights with a level and book the readings using the height of collimation method.

sections.heading: What surveying does
sections.text: Surveying fixes the position and height of points on the ground. Engineers use it to map sites, plan routes, calculate earthworks and set out structures. Two rules apply to all surveys: work from the whole to the part, and include independent checks.

sections.heading: How levelling works
sections.text:
A level gives a horizontal line of sight. A graduated staff is held on each point and read. A lower point gives a larger reading.

The reduced level (RL) is the height above a chosen datum, often mean sea level. A benchmark is a point whose level is known.

A backsight (BS) is the first reading after setting up the instrument. A foresight (FS) is the last reading before moving it. Any reading in between is an intermediate sight (IS). A change point is a firm point where both an FS and a new BS are taken.

The height of collimation (HPC) is the height of the line of sight:
HPC = RL + BS
RL = HPC − IS or FS

The rise and fall method is an alternative way to book the same readings.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
The benchmark has RL 100.000 m.

Setup 1:
BS on benchmark = 1.525, so HPC = 101.525
IS at P = 2.030, so RL of P = 99.495
FS at Q = 0.875, so RL of Q = 100.650

Setup 2:
BS on Q = 1.640, so HPC = 102.290
FS at R = 2.310, so RL of R = 99.980

Check:
ΣBS − ΣFS = 3.165 − 3.185 = −0.020
Last RL − first RL = 99.980 − 100.000 = −0.020

The two agree, so the arithmetic is correct. This check tests only the arithmetic, not the field readings. To test the fieldwork, close the run on a known benchmark. Intermediate sights are not in the check, so read them with extra care.

Keep backsight and foresight distances about equal. This cancels the collimation error of the instrument.

keyPoints: Height of collimation = reduced level + backsight.
Reduced level = height of collimation − staff reading.
A lower point gives a larger staff reading.
Check: ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL.
Equal backsight and foresight distances cancel collimation error.

en.title: Surveying: traversing, GNSS and setting out
en.short: Using angles and distances to fix positions, closing a traverse, and setting out works on site.

sections.heading: Instruments
sections.text:
A theodolite measures horizontal and vertical angles. A total station adds electronic distance measurement and stores the data. GNSS receivers find position from satellites. GPS is the best known of these satellite systems. Heights from GNSS need care, because satellites give height above a mathematical surface and not above mean sea level.

A bearing is the direction of a line, measured clockwise from north, from 0° to 360°.

sections.heading: Coordinates and closure of a traverse
sections.text:
A traverse is a connected series of lines with measured lengths and angles. It provides control points for a site.

For a line of length L on bearing θ:
Change in east (departure) = L sin θ
Change in north (latitude) = L cos θ

Example: L = 100 m on bearing 060°.
Departure = 100 × sin 60° = 86.60 m
Latitude = 100 × cos 60° = 50.00 m

A closed traverse returns to its start or ends on another known point, so it can be checked in two ways.

Angle check: the interior angles of a closed polygon with n sides total (n − 2) × 180°. For 5 sides, this is 540°. If the measured sum is 540°00′30″, the error is 30″, so each angle is reduced by 6″.

Linear check: suppose the coordinates miss closure by 0.06 m east and 0.08 m north.
Linear misclosure = √(0.06² + 0.08²) = 0.10 m
For a perimeter of 1,000 m, the precision is 0.10 ÷ 1,000 = 1 in 10,000.

The Bowditch method then shares the misclosure among the lines in proportion to their lengths.

sections.heading: Setting out
sections.text: Setting out transfers a design from the drawing to the ground. Engineers mark building corners, road centre lines and levels using pegs, profile boards and a total station. Control points must be placed where construction won’t disturb them, and they should be checked often. Always measure a final check distance between the pegs you have set. This catches errors before concrete is poured.

keyPoints: Departure = L sin θ and latitude = L cos θ, with bearings measured clockwise from north.
Interior angles of a closed traverse total (n − 2) × 180°.
Linear misclosure = √(ΔE² + ΔN²).
The Bowditch method shares misclosure in proportion to line length.
Always make an independent check after setting out.

en.title: Fluid properties and hydrostatics
en.short: Density, viscosity, pressure at depth, and the force of still water on gates and walls.

sections.heading: Fluid properties
sections.text:
A fluid is a substance that deforms continuously under a shear force, however small.

Density ρ is mass per unit volume. Water has ρ of about 1,000 kg/m³. Unit weight is γ = ρg, about 9.81 kN/m³ for water.

Viscosity is a fluid’s resistance to flow. Dynamic viscosity μ relates shear stress to the rate of change of velocity. Kinematic viscosity is ν = μ ÷ ρ, about 1 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s for water at 20 °C.

sections.heading: Pressure at depth
sections.text:
In a still liquid, pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh. Pressure at a point acts equally in all directions, and it acts at right angles to any surface it touches.

Example: at a depth of 5 m in water,
p = 1,000 × 9.81 × 5 = 49,050 Pa = 49.05 kPa.

This is gauge pressure, measured above atmospheric pressure. Absolute pressure adds about 101 kPa. Pressure is often described as a head, h = p ÷ (ρg), as measured by piezometers.

sections.heading: Force on a submerged surface
sections.text:
The resultant force on a plane surface is F = ρg × hc × A, where hc is the depth of the centroid of the surface and A is its area. The force acts at the centre of pressure. This point lies below the centroid, because pressure increases with depth.

Example: a vertical rectangular gate is 3 m wide and 4 m high, with water level at its top edge.
Area = 3 × 4 = 12 m²
Depth of centroid = 2 m
F = 1,000 × 9.81 × 2 × 12 = 235,440 N = 235.4 kN
With its top at the surface, the centre of pressure is at two-thirds of the depth: 2/3 × 4 = 2.67 m.

sections.heading: Buoyancy
sections.text: Archimedes’ principle states that the upward force on a submerged body equals the weight of fluid it displaces. Buoyancy can lift an empty underground tank when the water table is high, so designers must check for uplift.

keyPoints: Pressure at depth is p = ρgh.
Water has density of about 1,000 kg/m³ and unit weight of about 9.81 kN/m³.
Force on a plane surface = ρg × centroid depth × area.
The centre of pressure lies below the centroid.
Buoyancy can lift empty underground tanks, so check for uplift.

en.title: Shear force and bending moment diagrams
en.short: Finding and drawing internal shear force and bending moment along a beam.

sections.heading: Internal forces
sections.text:
Cut a beam at a section. To keep each part in equilibrium, the section carries internal forces. The shear force V is the sum of the vertical forces on one side of the cut. The bending moment M is the sum of the moments of those forces about the cut.

A common convention takes sagging moment as positive. Books differ on how to plot moments, so state your convention.

The three quantities are linked:
dV/dx = −w and dM/dx = V, where w is the downward load per unit length.

Where there is no load, V is constant and M is a straight line. Under a uniform load, V is a sloping line and M is a parabola. M reaches a maximum where V is zero or changes sign.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Use the 6 m beam with a 30 kN load at 2 m from A and 5 kN/m over the span. The reactions are RA = 35 kN and RB = 25 kN.

For 0 < x < 2: V = 35 − 5x, so V = 25 kN just left of the load.

For 2 < x < 6:
V = 35 − 30 − 5x = 5 − 5x
Just right of the point load, V = −5 kN. At x = 6, V = −25 kN, which matches RB.

V changes sign at the point load, so the maximum moment is at x = 2 m:
M = (35 × 2) − (5 × 2 × 1) = 70 − 10 = 60 kN·m

Check from the right: M = (25 × 4) − (5 × 4 × 2) = 100 − 40 = 60 kN·m. They agree.

sections.heading: Standard results
sections.text:
Simple span, uniform w: Mmax = wL²/8
Simple span, central load P: Mmax = PL/4
Cantilever, end load P: Mmax = PL
Cantilever, uniform w: Mmax = wL²/2

A point of contraflexure is where the moment changes sign.

keyPoints: Shear force is the slope of the bending moment diagram.
Maximum moment occurs where shear force is zero or changes sign.
Simply supported with uniform load: Mmax = wL²/8.
Simply supported with central point load: Mmax = PL/4.
Cantilever with end load: Mmax = PL at the support.
State your sign convention, because books differ.

en.title: Bending stress, shear stress and deflection
en.short: Section properties, the bending equation, shear stress and how far beams deflect.

sections.heading: Bending stress
sections.text:
A beam that sags is compressed on top and stretched at the bottom. Between them lies the neutral axis, where bending stress is zero. For an elastic beam of one material, the neutral axis passes through the centroid.

The bending equation is M ÷ I = σ ÷ y = E ÷ R, where I is the second moment of area, y is the distance from the neutral axis and R is the radius of curvature. The maximum stress is σ = M ÷ Z, where Z = I ÷ ymax is the elastic section modulus.

For a rectangle of breadth b and depth d: I = bd³/12 and Z = bd²/6. Depth matters most.

Example: a 200 mm × 400 mm section carries M = 60 kN·m.
Z = 200 × 400² ÷ 6 = 5.333 × 10⁶ mm³
σ = 60 × 10⁶ ÷ (5.333 × 10⁶) = 11.25 N/mm²

sections.heading: Shear stress
sections.text:
Shear stress in a beam is τ = VQ ÷ (Ib), where Q is the first moment of the area beyond the level considered. In a rectangle, it is zero at the top and bottom and greatest at the neutral axis, where τmax = 1.5V ÷ A.

For the same section with V = 35 kN:
τmax = 1.5 × 35,000 ÷ 80,000 = 0.66 N/mm².

sections.heading: Deflection
sections.text:
Deflection follows from EI d²y/dx² = M, where EI is the flexural rigidity. Macaulay’s method and the moment-area method organise the integration.

A simply supported beam under a uniform load deflects by δ = 5wL⁴ ÷ (384EI) at mid-span.

Example: w = 10 kN/m = 10 N/mm, L = 6,000 mm, E = 200,000 N/mm², I = 1.0 × 10⁸ mm⁴.
δ = 5 × 10 × 6,000⁴ ÷ (384 × 200,000 × 1.0 × 10⁸) = 8.44 mm

A limit such as span ÷ 360 gives 16.7 mm here. Actual limits depend on the code and the use.

keyPoints: Bending equation: M ÷ I = σ ÷ y = E ÷ R.
For a rectangle, I = bd³/12 and Z = bd²/6.
Maximum shear stress in a rectangle is 1.5V ÷ A.
Mid-span deflection under uniform load is 5wL⁴ ÷ (384EI).
Convert all quantities to N and mm before calculating.

en.title: Structural analysis: trusses and determinacy
en.short: Testing whether a structure is determinate, and finding truss forces by joints and sections.

sections.heading: Determinate or indeterminate
sections.text:
A structure is statically determinate when equilibrium alone can find all its forces. It is indeterminate when there are more unknowns than equations.

For a plane pin-jointed truss, with m members, r reactions and j joints:
If m + r = 2j, the truss may be determinate.
If m + r > 2j, it is indeterminate.
If m + r < 2j, it is a mechanism.

A truss can pass this count and still be unstable, so inspect its shape too.

sections.heading: How trusses work
sections.text:
A truss is a frame of straight members joined to form triangles. Roofs and bridges use it because it spans far with little material. In the ideal model, joints are frictionless pins and loads act only at joints. Each member then carries only axial tension or compression.

The method of joints applies ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 at each joint in turn. Start at a joint with no more than two unknowns.

The method of sections cuts through no more than three unknown members and applies equilibrium to one part. It suits a few chosen members.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
A triangular truss has a pin at A (0, 0), a roller at B (8, 0) and an apex at C (4, 3), in metres. A 60 kN load acts downward at C.

Count: m = 3, r = 3, j = 3, so m + r = 6 = 2j.

By symmetry, RA = RB = 30 kN.

Member AC has length √(4² + 3²) = 5 m, so sin θ = 3/5 and cos θ = 4/5.

At joint A, assume both member forces are tension:
Vertical: 30 + FAC × 0.6 = 0, so FAC = −50 kN, which is compression.
Horizontal: FAB + FAC × 0.8 = 0, so FAB = 40 kN, which is tension.

Check at joint C: the vertical components total 2 × 50 × 0.6 = 60 kN upward, which balances the load.

keyPoints: For a plane truss, test m + r against 2j.
Passing the count doesn’t prove stability, so inspect the shape.
Ideal truss members carry only axial tension or compression.
Use joints for all member forces and sections for a few chosen ones.
A negative answer means the assumed tension is really compression.

en.title: Indeterminate structures and moment distribution
en.short: Why continuous beams and frames need extra equations, with moment distribution worked through.

sections.heading: Why extra equations are needed
sections.text:
A continuous beam or a rigid frame has more unknowns than equilibrium equations. The extra equations come from compatibility: the deformed members must still fit together.

Moments are often smaller and there are other load paths, but support settlement and temperature change can produce extra forces.

Hand methods include the force method, slope-deflection and moment distribution. Computers use the stiffness method.

sections.heading: Moment distribution
sections.text:
Hardy Cross developed this method.

1. Lock all joints and find the fixed end moments from standard results.
2. Release one joint. Share the unbalanced moment using distribution factors: member stiffness ÷ total stiffness at the joint.
3. Carry half of each distributed moment to the far end, if that end is fixed.
4. Repeat until the changes are small.

A member’s stiffness is 4EI/L if the far end is fixed and 3EI/L if the far end is pinned.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
A continuous beam ABC has pinned supports at A, B and C. AB = 6 m and BC = 4 m, EI is constant and the load is 20 kN/m on both spans. Find the moment at B.

Stiffness: BA = 3EI/6 = 0.50EI and BC = 3EI/4 = 0.75EI
Distribution factors: 0.50 ÷ 1.25 = 0.4 and 0.75 ÷ 1.25 = 0.6

Fixed end moments for a span with the far end pinned (wL²/8):
BA = 20 × 6² ÷ 8 = 90 kN·m
BC = 20 × 4² ÷ 8 = 40 kN·m

Unbalanced moment = 90 − 40 = 50 kN·m
BA changes by 0.4 × 50 = 20, giving 90 − 20 = 70 kN·m
BC changes by 0.6 × 50 = 30, giving 40 + 30 = 70 kN·m

The hogging moment at B is 70 kN·m.

Check with the three-moment theorem:
2MB(6 + 4) = (20 × 6³ ÷ 4) + (20 × 4³ ÷ 4) = 1,080 + 320 = 1,400, so MB = 70 kN·m.

keyPoints: Indeterminate structures need compatibility as well as equilibrium.
Stiffness is 4EI/L with a fixed far end and 3EI/L with a pinned far end.
A distribution factor is the member’s stiffness divided by the joint’s total.
The carry-over factor to a fixed far end is one half.
Support settlement causes forces in indeterminate structures.

en.title: Reinforced concrete: limit states and beam design
en.short: Limit state ideas and designing a singly reinforced beam, using BS 8110 as the teaching example.

sections.heading: Why concrete is reinforced
sections.text: Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension. Steel bars are placed where tension occurs, and they carry the tension after the concrete cracks. The two materials work together because they bond well and expand at similar rates with temperature. Cover, the concrete outside the bars, protects the steel against corrosion and fire.

sections.heading: Limit state design
sections.text:
A limit state is a condition in which a structure stops doing its job. Ultimate limit states concern collapse. Serviceability limit states concern deflection, cracking and vibration.

Partial factors are applied to loads and materials. BS 8110 uses an ultimate load of 1.4Gk + 1.6Qk for dead and imposed loads, in the basic case. Eurocodes use 1.35Gk + 1.5Qk in the basic case. Don’t mix rules from different codes.

BS 8110 was withdrawn in the UK in 2010 and replaced by Eurocode 2, BS EN 1992. BS 8110 remains common in teaching and practice in Nigeria and other countries. Check which code applies where you work.

sections.heading: Worked example: singly reinforced beam
sections.text:
This uses the BS 8110 textbook method, with steel stress 0.87fy (partial factor 1.15). BS 8110:1997 first used 1.05, giving 0.95fy, until a 2005 amendment. Given: b = 250 mm, d = 450 mm, M = 150 kN·m, fcu = 25 N/mm², fy = 460 N/mm².

K = M ÷ (fcu b d²) = 150 × 10⁶ ÷ (25 × 250 × 450²) = 0.1185
K is below 0.156 (the limit with up to 10% redistribution), so compression steel is not required.

z = d[0.5 + √(0.25 − K ÷ 0.9)]
z = 450[0.5 + √(0.25 − 0.1317)] = 379.8 mm
The limit is 0.95d = 427.5 mm, so z = 379.8 mm applies.

As = M ÷ (0.87 fy z) = 150 × 10⁶ ÷ (0.87 × 460 × 379.8) = 987 mm²
Provide 4 bars of 20 mm diameter, with area 1,257 mm².

Shear links, deflection, bar spacing, anchorage and minimum steel must still be checked.

keyPoints: Steel carries the tension and concrete carries the compression.
Ultimate limit states concern collapse, and serviceability limit states concern use.
BS 8110 basic ultimate load is 1.4Gk + 1.6Qk, and Eurocodes use 1.35Gk + 1.5Qk.
In BS 8110, with up to 10% redistribution, K above 0.156 calls for compression steel.
Codes differ by country, so never mix rules from different codes.

en.title: Reinforced concrete: slabs and columns
en.short: One-way and two-way slabs, short and slender columns, with worked load and capacity examples.

sections.heading: Slabs
sections.text:
A slab is a flat plate that carries load to beams, walls or columns. For slabs supported on all four sides, the ratio of long span to short span decides the behaviour. If the ratio exceeds about 2, the slab bends mainly across the short span and is treated as one-way. Otherwise it is two-way, with main steel in both directions.

Slabs are designed per metre width, using the same bending method as beams. Deflection often controls the depth. Punching shear around columns is critical in flat slabs.

Example: a one-way simply supported slab spans 4 m. The dead load is 5 kN/m², including self-weight, and the imposed load is 3 kN/m². A 150 mm slab alone weighs about 0.15 × 24 = 3.6 kN/m².
Ultimate load (BS 8110) = 1.4 × 5 + 1.6 × 3 = 11.8 kN/m²
Moment per metre width = 11.8 × 4² ÷ 8 = 23.6 kN·m per metre

sections.heading: Columns
sections.text:
Columns carry mainly compression, usually with some bending. A column is braced if walls or bracing resist sideways movement of the frame, and unbraced if it must resist that movement itself.

A column is short or slender according to the ratio of effective height to section dimension. Short columns fail by crushing of the materials. Slender columns also bend sideways, which adds moment.

Links hold the main bars in place and prevent them from buckling.

sections.heading: Worked example: short braced column
sections.text:
BS 8110 textbooks give, for a short braced column with small moments (BS 8110:1997 as first issued has 0.8, not 0.75):
N = 0.4 fcu Ac + 0.75 fy Asc

Given: 300 mm × 300 mm, fcu = 30 N/mm², fy = 460 N/mm², 4 bars of 20 mm (Asc = 1,257 mm²).
Ac = 90,000 − 1,257 = 88,743 mm²
Concrete: 0.4 × 30 × 88,743 = 1,064,916 N
Steel: 0.75 × 460 × 1,257 = 433,665 N
N = 1,498,581 N, or about 1,499 kN

keyPoints: A long-to-short span ratio above about 2 means one-way action.
Slabs are designed per metre width.
Punching shear around columns is critical in flat slabs.
Slender columns suffer added moment from sideways bending.
Include self-weight, which is often the largest load on a slab.

en.title: Structural steel design and buckling
en.short: Steel sections, tension and compression members, Euler buckling, beams and connections.

sections.heading: Steel as a material
sections.text:
Structural steel has a high strength-to-weight ratio, good ductility and reliable properties. Common grades include S275 and S355, where the number is the nominal yield strength in N/mm² for thinner sections. Hot-rolled sections include universal beams, universal columns, channels and angles. Corrosion and fire protection must be planned.

Codes include BS 5950, withdrawn in the UK in 2010 but still taught, and Eurocode 3, BS EN 1993. Other countries have their own codes, and South Africa, for example, has its own national steel standard.

sections.heading: Buckling of compression members
sections.text:
A slender member in compression can bow sideways suddenly, well below its squash load. The Euler critical load for an ideal column is:
Pcr = π²EI ÷ Le²

I is the smaller second moment of area, and Le is the effective length. In theory, Le equals L for pin-pin ends, 0.5L for fixed-fixed, about 0.7L for fixed-pinned, and 2L for a cantilever. Design codes may give different values.

Example: E = 210,000 N/mm², I = 1.5 × 10⁷ mm⁴, Le = 3,000 mm, A = 6,000 mm², grade S275.
Pcr = π² × 210,000 × 1.5 × 10⁷ ÷ 3,000² = 3,454 kN
Squash load = 6,000 × 275 = 1,650 kN
Radius of gyration r = √(I ÷ A) = 50 mm
Slenderness = Le ÷ r = 60

The Euler load exceeds the squash load, so the Euler formula alone is unsafe here. Real columns have imperfections and residual stresses. Codes therefore provide buckling curves that give a lower design strength.

sections.heading: Beams and connections
sections.text:
A steel beam must be checked for bending, shear, deflection and local buckling of thin plates. An I-section with an unrestrained compression flange can also twist and move sideways. This is lateral torsional buckling. Restraint from a floor slab or from bracing prevents it.

Tension members must be checked on their net area at bolt holes. Connections use bolts or welds. They deserve as much care as the members.

keyPoints: Euler critical load is Pcr = π²EI ÷ Le², using the smaller I.
Slenderness = effective length ÷ radius of gyration.
Real columns fail below the Euler load, so codes use buckling curves.
Unrestrained beams can fail by lateral torsional buckling.
Check tension members on net area at bolt holes.

en.title: Engineering geology: rocks, structures and ground conditions
en.short: Rock types, weathering, faults and groundwater, and how geology affects sites and works.

sections.heading: Why geology matters
sections.text:
Every civil engineering work rests on or in the ground, so its safety depends on what lies below the surface. Engineering geology applies knowledge of rocks and their history to sites, foundations, tunnels, dams and slopes.

Rocks fall into three groups. Igneous rocks, such as granite and basalt, form when molten rock cools. Sedimentary rocks, such as sandstone, shale and limestone, form in layers from deposited material. Shale can soften in water, and limestone can dissolve and leave cavities. Metamorphic rocks, such as marble, schist and gneiss, form when heat and pressure change an older rock. Schist can split along its layers.

sections.heading: Structures, weathering and water
sections.text:
A fault is a fracture along which the rock on each side has moved. A joint is a fracture with little or no movement. These features often control strength and water flow more than the intact rock does. Layers or joints that dip towards a cutting can let a slope slide.

Weathering breaks rock down by physical or chemical action. Soil that stays where it formed is called residual soil, and hot, wet climates can produce deep weathering and lateritic soils. Transported soils were carried by rivers, wind, ice or the sea.

The groundwater level affects excavations, foundations and slope stability.

sections.heading: Worked example: rock quality designation
sections.text:
A site investigation uses geological maps, trial pits, boreholes and rock coring. Rock quality designation (RQD) describes how fractured a rock mass is. It is the total length of sound core pieces longer than 100 mm, as a percentage of the length of the core run.

A 1.5 m core run contains sound pieces of 300, 220, 150 and 130 mm. Other pieces are shorter than 100 mm.
Total = 300 + 220 + 150 + 130 = 800 mm
RQD = 800 ÷ 1,500 × 100 = 53%

As a rough guide, RQD above 75% suggests good rock and below 50% suggests poor rock. This result lies between them, so the rock needs further assessment.

keyPoints: Rocks are grouped as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic.
A fault has moved along its fracture, and a joint has little or no movement.
Joints and layers often control rock strength and water flow.
Residual soil stays where it formed, and transported soil has been moved.
RQD = length of sound core pieces longer than 100 mm ÷ core run length × 100.

en.title: Soil mechanics: properties and classification
en.short: Soil phases, void ratio, Atterberg limits, classification and compaction.

sections.heading: Soil as three phases
sections.text:
Soil is made of solid grains, water and air. The key terms are:
Moisture content: w = mass of water ÷ mass of solids
Void ratio: e = volume of voids ÷ volume of solids
Porosity: n = voids ÷ total volume = e ÷ (1 + e)
Degree of saturation: S = volume of water ÷ volume of voids
Specific gravity of solids: Gs, about 2.65 for many soils

A useful link is Se = wGs.

sections.heading: Classifying soils
sections.text:
A sieve analysis measures grain sizes in coarse soils, and a hydrometer test in fine soils.

The Atterberg limits describe clays and silts. The liquid limit (LL) is the moisture content at which a soil starts to flow. The plastic limit (PL) is the moisture content at which it starts to crumble when rolled. The plasticity index is PI = LL − PL. Classification systems include the Unified system, the AASHTO system for roads and the British system.

Lateritic soils are widely used in road construction in tropical Africa. Black cotton soils, found in parts of northern Nigeria, Kenya and elsewhere, swell when wet and shrink when dry. They can crack light buildings and roads.

sections.heading: Compaction
sections.text: Compaction removes air from soil by mechanical energy. A laboratory Proctor test plots dry density against moisture content. The peak gives the maximum dry density and the optimum moisture content, which control earthworks on site.

keyPoints: Soil consists of solids, water and air.
The relation Se = wGs links saturation, void ratio and moisture content.
Plasticity index = liquid limit − plastic limit.
Compaction removes air, and the Proctor test gives the target density.
Black cotton soils swell and shrink, which can damage light structures.

en.title: Effective stress, seepage, consolidation and shear strength
en.short: The central ideas of soil behaviour: effective stress, Darcy’s law, settlement and Mohr-Coulomb strength.

sections.heading: Effective stress
sections.text:
Terzaghi’s principle says that effective stress σ′ controls soil strength and compression:
σ′ = σ − u
where σ is the total stress and u is the pore water pressure.

Example: 2 m of sand with γ = 18 kN/m³ lies above the water table, on 3 m of saturated soil with γ = 20 kN/m³. At a depth of 5 m:
σ = (2 × 18) + (3 × 20) = 96 kPa
u = 3 × 9.81 = 29.43 kPa
σ′ = 96 − 29.43 = 66.57 kPa

A rise in water level can trigger a slope failure: u increases, so σ′ and strength both fall.

sections.heading: Seepage
sections.text: Water flows through soil according to Darcy’s law: v = ki, where k is the coefficient of permeability and i is the hydraulic gradient. Gravels have a far higher k than clays. Flow nets estimate seepage under dams and sheet piles.

sections.heading: Consolidation
sections.text:
A load on saturated clay first raises the pore pressure. As water slowly drains, stress moves to the grains and the clay settles. This process, consolidation, can take years.

Settlement can be estimated from an oedometer test: S = mv × Δσ′ × H, where mv is the coefficient of volume compressibility.

Example: H = 4 m, mv = 0.0002 m²/kN, Δσ′ = 50 kPa.
S = 0.0002 × 50 × 4 = 0.04 m = 40 mm

The time is t = Tv d² ÷ cv, where d is the longest drainage path and cv the coefficient of consolidation, with Tv about 0.197 for 50% consolidation and 0.848 for 90%.

sections.heading: Shear strength
sections.text:
The Mohr-Coulomb criterion is τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′, with cohesion intercept c′ and friction angle φ′.

Example: c′ = 10 kPa, σ′ = 100 kPa, φ′ = 30°.
τ = 10 + 100 tan 30° = 67.7 kPa

The shear box and triaxial tests measure these values. Short-term clay loading often uses undrained strength cu.

keyPoints: Effective stress: σ′ = σ − u.
Effective stress controls soil strength and compression.
Darcy’s law: v = ki.
Consolidation settlement: S = mv × Δσ′ × H.
Mohr-Coulomb strength: τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′.

en.title: Foundations and retaining walls
en.short: Shallow and deep foundations, bearing capacity, settlement checks and earth pressure on walls.

sections.heading: Choosing a foundation
sections.text:
A foundation transfers load safely to the ground. Every design begins with a site investigation, including boreholes, trial pits and laboratory tests.

Shallow foundations include pad footings under columns, strip footings under walls, and rafts that cover the whole building area. Piles carry the load through weak soil to stronger layers. Soft ground in parts of Lagos often requires piles or rafts for heavier buildings.

The soil must not fail in shear, and settlement must be tolerable. Differential settlement between parts of a building causes more damage than uniform settlement.

sections.heading: Worked example: bearing capacity
sections.text:
Terzaghi’s equation for a strip footing is:
qult = cNc + γDNq + 0.5γBNγ

For undrained clay (φ = 0), Terzaghi’s factors are Nc = 5.7, Nq = 1 and Nγ = 0. Other authors use 5.14 for Nc, so check your course notes.

Given: cu = 60 kPa, γ = 18 kN/m³, depth D = 1 m.
qult = (5.7 × 60) + (18 × 1 × 1) = 342 + 18 = 360 kPa
Using a factor of safety of 3: qa = 360 ÷ 3 = 120 kPa

For a wall load of 300 kN/m: B = 300 ÷ 120 = 2.5 m

A full design also includes the footing’s weight, and codes differ in their factors.

sections.heading: Retaining walls
sections.text:
A retaining wall holds back soil. For level, cohesionless ground and a smooth wall, Rankine’s active coefficient is:
Ka = (1 − sin φ) ÷ (1 + sin φ)
The total thrust is Pa = ½KaγH², acting at H/3 above the base.

Example: φ = 30°, γ = 18 kN/m³, H = 4 m.
Ka = 0.5 ÷ 1.5 = 1/3
Pa = 0.5 × 1/3 × 18 × 4² = 48 kN/m of wall, 1.33 m above the base

A gravity wall is checked against sliding, overturning and bearing failure. Drainage is essential, because water pressure greatly increases the thrust.

keyPoints: Foundations must satisfy both bearing capacity and settlement limits.
Differential settlement causes the most damage.
Terzaghi’s equation: qult = cNc + γDNq + 0.5γBNγ.
Rankine active coefficient: Ka = (1 − sin φ) ÷ (1 + sin φ).
Retaining walls need drainage to limit water pressure.

en.title: Fluid flow: continuity, Bernoulli and pipes
en.short: The equations of moving water, friction losses in pipes, and the power needed to pump.

sections.heading: Continuity and Bernoulli
sections.text:
For steady flow of an incompressible fluid, the discharge Q stays constant along a pipe:
Q = A₁V₁ = A₂V₂

Bernoulli’s equation expresses energy per unit weight of fluid, called head:
p ÷ (ρg) + V² ÷ (2g) + z = constant

The three terms are the pressure head, the velocity head and the elevation head. The equation assumes steady, frictionless flow along a streamline. Real pipes lose energy, so a head loss term hf is added.

sections.heading: Laminar and turbulent flow
sections.text:
The Reynolds number compares inertia with viscosity:
Re = VD ÷ ν

In pipes, flow is usually laminar when Re is below about 2,000, and turbulent above about 4,000. Most water supply pipes run turbulent.

Friction head loss is given by the Darcy-Weisbach equation:
hf = fLV² ÷ (2gD)

The friction factor f depends on Re and on pipe roughness, and it can be read from a Moody chart. For laminar flow, f = 64 ÷ Re. Some older British books write 4f, with a smaller f, so check your text. Bends and valves add minor losses, written as kV² ÷ (2g).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
A pipeline supplying a town near Kumasi has D = 0.3 m, L = 500 m and Q = 0.1 m³/s, with f = 0.02. A pump lifts water through a static height of 20 m, with efficiency 75%. Ignore minor losses.

A = π × 0.3² ÷ 4 = 0.0707 m²
V = 0.1 ÷ 0.0707 = 1.415 m/s
Re = 1.415 × 0.3 ÷ (1 × 10⁻⁶) = 4.2 × 10⁵, so the flow is turbulent
hf = 0.02 × 500 × 1.415² ÷ (2 × 9.81 × 0.3) = 3.40 m
Total head = 20 + 3.40 = 23.40 m
Water power = ρgQH = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.1 × 23.40 = 22.96 kW
Input power = 22.96 ÷ 0.75 = 30.6 kW

A larger pipe costs more but can save pumping energy for years.

keyPoints: Continuity: Q = AV is constant along a pipe.
Bernoulli: pressure head + velocity head + elevation head = constant, without losses.
Reynolds number: Re = VD ÷ ν.
Darcy-Weisbach: hf = fLV² ÷ (2gD).
Pump power = ρgQH ÷ efficiency.

en.title: Open channel flow
en.short: Flow with a free surface: Manning’s equation, Froude number, hydraulic jumps and weirs.

sections.heading: Uniform flow
sections.text:
Rivers, canals and road drains have a free water surface, and gravity drives the flow. In uniform flow, the depth and velocity stay the same along the channel, and the water surface runs parallel to the bed.

Manning’s equation, in SI units, gives the velocity:
V = (1 ÷ n) × R^(2/3) × S^(1/2)

Here n is Manning’s roughness coefficient, about 0.015 for finished concrete and higher for natural channels. S is the bed slope. R is the hydraulic radius, equal to the flow area divided by the wetted perimeter. The wetted perimeter is the length of the channel boundary in contact with water.

The most efficient rectangular section has breadth equal to twice the depth.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
A concrete rectangular channel has breadth 3 m and flow depth 1.5 m, with n = 0.015 and S = 0.001.

A = 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 m²
P = 3 + (2 × 1.5) = 6 m
R = 4.5 ÷ 6 = 0.75 m
V = 66.67 × 0.8255 × 0.03162 = 1.74 m/s
Q = 1.74 × 4.5 = 7.83 m³/s

Froude number = V ÷ √(gy) = 1.74 ÷ √(9.81 × 1.5) = 0.45
This is below 1, so the flow is subcritical.

sections.heading: Critical flow and control structures
sections.text:
The Froude number compares the flow speed with the speed of a small surface wave. Flow is subcritical when Fr < 1, critical when Fr = 1 and supercritical when Fr > 1. Subcritical flow is deep and slow, while supercritical flow is shallow and fast.

When fast supercritical flow meets slower subcritical flow, a hydraulic jump forms. This is a sudden rise in water level with turbulence, and it dissipates energy. Designers use jumps below dam spillways to protect the riverbed.

Weirs and flumes measure discharge. A sharp-crested rectangular weir has Q = (2/3)Cd b √(2g) H^(3/2), where H is the head above the crest. Culverts carry water under roads.

keyPoints: Hydraulic radius = flow area ÷ wetted perimeter.
Froude number: Fr = V ÷ √(gy).
Fr < 1 is subcritical, and Fr > 1 is supercritical.
A hydraulic jump dissipates energy.

en.title: Hydrology: rainfall, runoff and flood estimation
en.short: The hydrological cycle, measuring rainfall, the rational method, hydrographs and return periods.

sections.heading: The water balance
sections.text:
Hydrology studies water as it moves through the environment. The cycle includes evaporation, transpiration by plants, precipitation, infiltration into the ground, surface runoff and groundwater flow. For a catchment, which is the land area draining to one point, the water balance is:
P = Q + E + ΔS
P is precipitation, Q is runoff, E is evapotranspiration and ΔS is the change in storage.

Average catchment rainfall can be estimated from the mean of the gauges, Thiessen polygons or isohyets (lines of equal rainfall).

sections.heading: Estimating peak runoff
sections.text:
A hydrograph plots discharge against time at a point on a river. A unit hydrograph is the response of a catchment to one unit of effective rainfall, such as 1 cm, falling in a set time. It lets engineers predict a flood from a design storm.

For small catchments, the rational method gives the peak flow:
Q = 0.278 C i A
Q is in m³/s, C is a runoff coefficient, i is the rainfall intensity in mm/h and A is the area in km². The intensity is taken for a storm lasting as long as the time of concentration. This is the time water takes to travel from the farthest point of the catchment.

Example: an urban catchment in Accra has A = 2 km², C = 0.6, i = 60 mm/h.
Q = 0.278 × 0.6 × 60 × 2 = 20.0 m³/s

sections.heading: Return period and risk
sections.text:
The return period T is the average interval between events of a given size. The chance of being equalled or exceeded in any year is 1 ÷ T. A 50-year flood doesn’t come exactly every 50 years.

The chance of at least one exceedance in n years is 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ.

Example: T = 50 and n = 25.
Risk = 1 − 0.98²⁵ = 0.397, or about 40%

Groundwater is held in aquifers. Long-term pumping from boreholes must not exceed the recharge.

keyPoints: Water balance: P = Q + E + ΔS.
Rational method: Q = 0.278 C i A, for small catchments.
Use a storm duration equal to the time of concentration.
Annual exceedance probability is 1 ÷ T.
Risk over n years is 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ.

en.title: Water supply and treatment
en.short: Forecasting demand, treating raw water to drinking standard and distributing it to users.

sections.heading: Estimating demand
sections.text:
A water scheme starts with a forecast of population and use. Demand per person depends on income, climate and access. Urban values often lie between about 100 and 250 litres per person per day, but they vary widely, so use local data or the national standard. Demand also varies by season and by hour, so peak factors are applied. Leakage must be allowed for, as it can be a large share of supply.

Worked example: a town in Kenya has 50,000 people, with growth of 3% per year. Forecast 20 years ahead with the geometric method, using 120 L per person per day and a peak day factor of 1.8.
Future population = 50,000 × 1.03²⁰ = 50,000 × 1.806 = 90,306
Average demand = 90,306 × 0.12 m³ = 10,837 m³/day
Peak day demand = 10,837 × 1.8 ≈ 19,500 m³/day
In m³/s: 19,500 ÷ 86,400 = 0.226 m³/s

sections.heading: Treatment
sections.text:
A conventional surface water plant follows this order.

Screening removes large floating matter.
Coagulation adds a chemical such as alum, which neutralises the charge on fine particles.
Flocculation stirs gently, so that the particles clump into flocs.
Sedimentation lets the flocs settle.
Filtration through sand removes the remaining particles.
Disinfection, usually with chlorine, kills disease organisms. A small residual is kept to protect the water in the pipes.

Groundwater may need less treatment, but it can contain iron, fluoride or other dissolved substances. The WHO publishes drinking water guidelines, including that E. coli must not be detectable in a 100 mL sample. National standards build on these and can differ.

sections.heading: Distribution
sections.text: Water travels through mains from reservoirs and elevated tanks to consumers. Storage balances the steady supply from the plant against varying hourly demand, and it also provides a reserve for emergencies. A looped network gives better reliability than a branched one. Engineers analyse networks with the Hardy Cross method or software, and they check for adequate pressure at peak demand.

keyPoints: Geometric growth: future population = P₀(1 + r)ⁿ.
Peak factors and leakage must be added to average demand.
Usual order: screening, coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, disinfection.
A chlorine residual protects water in the pipes.
Looped networks are more reliable than branched ones.

en.title: Wastewater and environmental engineering
en.short: BOD, stages of sewage treatment, solid waste and environmental impact assessment.

sections.heading: Measuring pollution
sections.text:
Organic waste consumes oxygen as bacteria break it down. If a river loses too much dissolved oxygen, fish and other life die. Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) is the oxygen used by microorganisms, usually measured over 5 days at 20 °C. Chemical oxygen demand (COD) uses a strong chemical oxidant, and it is faster to measure. Other important measures are suspended solids, nutrients and faecal bacteria.

Worked example: a sample is diluted 1 in 50. The dissolved oxygen is 8.5 mg/L at the start and 4.5 mg/L after 5 days.
BOD₅ = (8.5 − 4.5) × 50 = 200 mg/L

A plant receives 10,000 m³/day of this sewage. Since 1 mg/L = 1 g/m³:
BOD load = 10,000 × 200 = 2,000,000 g/day = 2,000 kg/day
After 90% removal, the effluent has 200 × 0.1 = 20 mg/L.

sections.heading: Treatment stages
sections.text:
Preliminary treatment uses screens and grit channels to remove large solids. Primary treatment settles out suspended matter. Secondary treatment uses microorganisms to consume dissolved organic matter, for example in activated sludge plants or trickling filters. Tertiary treatment removes nutrients or further solids where the receiving water requires it. The sludge produced also needs safe treatment and disposal.

Waste stabilisation ponds use sunlight, algae and bacteria. They need a lot of land but little power and few skilled staff, so they suit warm climates where land is available. Septic tanks with soakaways serve many homes without sewers. They must be sited away from wells and boreholes, because they can pollute groundwater.

sections.heading: Solid waste and impact assessment
sections.text:
Solid waste management covers collection, recycling, composting, and disposal in engineered landfills. A landfill liner and a leachate collection system protect groundwater.

An environmental impact assessment predicts the effects of a project before it is approved, and it proposes ways to reduce them. Nigeria has an Environmental Impact Assessment Act, and many other countries have their own laws. Discharge limits also differ by country.

keyPoints: BOD measures oxygen used by microorganisms, usually over 5 days at 20 °C.
BOD load in g/day = flow in m³/day × concentration in mg/L.
Secondary treatment uses microorganisms to remove organic matter.
Stabilisation ponds suit warm climates with available land.
Site septic tanks away from wells and boreholes.

en.title: Highway engineering: planning and geometric design
en.short: Road classes, sight distance, horizontal and vertical curves, and drainage.

sections.heading: Planning a road
sections.text:
Roads are classified by function, from motorways and trunk roads to local access roads. Route selection balances the terrain, the soils, drainage, land use, cost and environmental effects. Geometric design then sets the layout from a design speed, which governs most dimensions.

The standards come from national manuals and bodies such as AASHTO in the USA. Their values differ, so use the document that applies to your country.

sections.heading: Sight distance
sections.text:
Drivers must see far enough ahead to stop safely. Stopping sight distance has two parts: the distance travelled while the driver reacts, and the braking distance.
SSD = vt + v² ÷ (2gf)
Here v is the speed in m/s, t is the reaction time and f is the coefficient of longitudinal friction.

Example: design speed 100 km/h, t = 2.5 s, f = 0.35.
v = 100 ÷ 3.6 = 27.78 m/s
Reaction distance = 27.78 × 2.5 = 69.4 m
Braking distance = 27.78² ÷ (2 × 9.81 × 0.35) = 112.4 m
SSD = 69.4 + 112.4 = 181.8 m

sections.heading: Curves
sections.text:
On a horizontal curve, the vehicle needs a sideways force. This comes from superelevation, which is the banking of the road, together with side friction:
e + f = V² ÷ (127R)
Here V is in km/h and R is the radius in metres.

Example: V = 80 km/h, e = 0.06, f = 0.14.
R = 80² ÷ (127 × 0.20) = 6,400 ÷ 25.4 = 252 m

A transition curve lets the curvature change gradually. Vertical curves are usually parabolic, and they connect two different gradients. Crest curves are mostly limited by sight distance. Sag curves are limited by headlight reach, comfort and drainage.

sections.heading: Cross-section and drainage
sections.text: The cross-section includes traffic lanes, shoulders, side slopes and ditches. A camber helps rainwater run off the surface. Water weakens the road base and is a main cause of pavement failure, so design drains and culverts from the start.

keyPoints: Design speed governs most geometric dimensions.
SSD = reaction distance + braking distance.
On curves: e + f = V² ÷ (127R).
Crest curves are mostly limited by sight distance.
Water is a main cause of pavement failure, so plan drainage early.

en.title: Pavement design and traffic engineering
en.short: Flexible and rigid pavements, CBR, standard axles, and the flow-density-speed relationship.

sections.heading: Pavement types
sections.text:
A pavement spreads wheel loads so that the natural ground, called the subgrade, isn’t overstressed. A flexible pavement has layers of bituminous surfacing, base and subbase, and it spreads load through its layers. A rigid pavement uses a concrete slab, which spreads the load by bending.

The California bearing ratio (CBR) test compares the penetration resistance of a soil with that of a standard crushed stone, expressed as a percentage. A weak subgrade with a low CBR needs a thicker pavement. Design charts are specific to each method and country.

sections.heading: Worked example: design traffic
sections.text:
Damage rises steeply with axle load. A widely used rule, the fourth power law, gives the damage factor as (axle load ÷ standard axle)⁴, with a standard axle of 80 kN in many methods.

A 120 kN axle: (120 ÷ 80)⁴ = 5.06 standard axles
So one axle overloaded by 50% does about five times the damage. This is why axle load control matters.

A road expects 300 heavy vehicles per day in the design lane in the first year. Each vehicle equals 2 standard axles on average. Traffic grows 5% per year over 20 years.
Growth factor = (1.05²⁰ − 1) ÷ 0.05 = 33.07
Design traffic = 300 × 2 × 365 × 33.07 = 7.24 million standard axles

sections.heading: Traffic flow
sections.text:
Traffic engineering studies vehicle movement. Three measures are linked:
q = k × v
where q is the flow in vehicles per hour, k is the density in vehicles per km and v is the mean speed in km/h.

Example: at k = 25 veh/km and v = 60 km/h, q = 1,500 veh/h.

As density rises, speed falls. Flow rises to a maximum, the capacity, and then falls as congestion builds.

Passenger car units convert mixed traffic to an equivalent number of cars, because a truck takes more road space than a car. Motorcycles and minibuses are important in many African cities, so local values are needed.

keyPoints: Flexible pavements spread load through layers, and rigid pavements spread it by slab bending.
A low CBR means a thicker pavement is required.
Damage rises with about the fourth power of axle load.
Traffic flow: q = k × v.
Capacity is the maximum flow, reached before congestion lowers it.

en.title: Construction planning and the critical path method
en.short: Breaking a project into activities, finding the critical path and float, and tracking progress.

sections.heading: Planning tools
sections.text:
Construction management delivers a project on time, within budget, to the required quality and safely. Planning starts by breaking the work into activities, then estimating the duration of each, then finding the order they must follow.

A Gantt or bar chart shows activities against time. It is easy to read, but it doesn’t show clearly how activities depend on one another. A network diagram shows those links. The critical path method (CPM) uses the network to find the longest path through a project, which sets the shortest possible project duration.

sections.heading: Worked example: critical path
sections.text:
A small project has these activities, with durations in weeks:
A: 3, no predecessor
B: 5, after A
C: 2, after A
D: 4, after C
E: 3, after B and D

Forward pass (earliest start and finish):
A: 0 to 3
B: 3 to 8
C: 3 to 5
D: 5 to 9
E: starts at the later of 8 and 9, so 9 to 12
The project takes 12 weeks.

Backward pass (latest finish and start):
E: 12, 9
D: 9, 5
B: 9, 4
C: 5, 3
A: 3, 0

Total float = latest start − earliest start:
B: 4 − 3 = 1 week
All the others: 0

The critical path is A, C, D, E, with total duration 3 + 2 + 4 + 3 = 12 weeks. A delay to any critical activity delays the project. Activity B can slip by 1 week.

sections.heading: Controlling progress
sections.text:
Plans need regular updating against actual progress. PERT is a related method that uses three duration estimates for uncertain activities. Resource levelling spreads labour and plant to avoid sharp peaks. Crashing shortens critical activities by spending more money, and it is worthwhile only while the savings exceed the cost.

Earned value analysis compares the planned cost, the actual cost and the budgeted value of the work done. It can show early that a project is heading for overspending or delay.

keyPoints: The critical path is the longest path through the network.
Total float = latest start − earliest start.
Critical activities have zero total float in a simple network.
Bar charts are easy to read but don’t clearly show dependency.
Crashing makes sense only while savings exceed the extra cost.

en.title: Estimating, contracts and site management
en.short: Quantities and bills of quantities, tendering, standard contract forms, quality and site safety.

sections.heading: Quantities and cost
sections.text:
A bill of quantities (BOQ) lists the measured work in a project, with a unit rate for each item. Quantity surveyors usually prepare it using a standard method of measurement. A rate includes labour, materials, plant, overheads and profit.

Worked example: a concrete strip foundation is 20 m long, 0.9 m wide and 0.2 m thick. Use the 1:2:4 mix, at 6.4 bags of cement per m³.
Volume = 20 × 0.9 × 0.2 = 3.6 m³
Cement = 3.6 × 6.4 = 23.04 bags, so order 24 bags plus waste
At an example price of 10,000 naira per bag, cement costs 240,000 naira.

Prices change quickly, so use current local rates in real estimates. The same method applies whether the rates are in naira, cedis, rand, shillings or pounds.

sections.heading: Tendering and contracts
sections.text:
In competitive tendering, contractors submit priced offers, and the client evaluates them on price and ability. Public works follow procurement law. Examples are Nigeria’s Public Procurement Act 2007 and Ghana’s Public Procurement Act 2003. Check the current versions, as such laws are amended.

A contract sets out who bears which risk, how variations are priced, how payments are made and how disputes are settled. Common standard forms include FIDIC for international works, and NEC and JCT in the UK. A traditional contract separates design from construction. In design and build, one firm does both. Payment usually follows interim certificates, with a percentage retained until defects are corrected.

sections.heading: Quality and safety on site
sections.text:
Quality control tests the materials and the work against the specification, such as cube tests and compaction tests. Keep clear records, because they are evidence if a problem appears later.

Common causes of serious injury include falls from height, collapsing excavations, moving plant and electric shock. Good practice includes a risk assessment for each task, safe scaffolding, shoring of deep trenches, protective equipment and training. Temporary works, such as formwork and props, need proper design too. Safety laws differ by country.

keyPoints: A BOQ lists measured work with a rate for each item.
A rate includes labour, materials, plant, overheads and profit.
Contracts allocate risk and set rules for variations and payment.
FIDIC is widely used internationally, and NEC and JCT are common in the UK.
Falls, excavation collapse, moving plant and electric shock are major site hazards.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and COREN
en.short: How engineers qualify and register, including COREN in Nigeria, and their duties to the public.

sections.heading: Regulation in Nigeria
sections.text:
In Nigeria, the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN) regulates engineering under the Engineers (Registration, etc.) Act. It registers four cadres: engineers, engineering technologists, engineering technicians and engineering craftsmen. It also registers engineering firms and accredits engineering programmes in Nigerian institutions.

The Nigerian Society of Engineers (NSE) is the main professional body. It is a membership organisation, while COREN is the statutory regulator.

Registration as an engineer generally requires a recognised qualification and supervised professional experience, followed by an assessment. These rules change, so read the current requirements from COREN itself.

sections.heading: Other countries
sections.text:
Each country has its own system, and a licence in one country doesn’t automatically permit practice in another.

Ghana: the Engineering Council of Ghana regulates practice under the Engineering Council Act, 2011 (Act 819). The Ghana Institution of Engineering (formerly of Engineers) is a leading professional body.
Kenya: the Engineers Board of Kenya.
South Africa: the Engineering Council of South Africa (ECSA).
UK: the Engineering Council sets the standards, and institutions such as the Institution of Civil Engineers (ICE) award grades such as Chartered Engineer (CEng).

sections.heading: Ethics and duties
Building a career
sections.text: Keep a logbook during industrial training, such as SIWES in Nigeria, because professional bodies often ask for evidence of experience.

keyPoints: COREN is Nigeria’s statutory regulator of engineering.
COREN registers engineers, technologists, technicians and craftsmen.
NSE is a professional society, and it is distinct from COREN.
A licence in one country doesn’t automatically allow practice in another.
The first duty of an engineer is to public safety, health and welfare.

en.title: Advanced structural analysis: the matrix stiffness method
en.short: How structural software works: element stiffness, assembly, boundary conditions and solution.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text:
The stiffness method takes joint displacements as the unknowns:
[K]{d} = {F}
[K] is the global stiffness matrix, {d} holds joint displacements and {F} joint loads. Each entry Kij is the force at degree of freedom i caused by a unit displacement at degree of freedom j, with all other displacements held at zero.

A degree of freedom is one independent way in which a joint can move. A joint in a plane frame has three: two translations and one rotation.

The method suits computers because the steps are the same for any structure. The flexibility method takes forces as unknowns and is harder to automate.

sections.heading: The steps
sections.text:
1. Number the joints and degrees of freedom.
2. Write each member’s stiffness matrix in its local axes.
3. Transform it to global axes using a rotation matrix: [k]global = [T]ᵀ[k]local[T].
4. Assemble the global matrix by adding terms at matching degrees of freedom.
5. Convert member loads to equivalent joint loads, using fixed end forces.
6. Apply the support conditions.
7. Solve for {d}.
8. Recover the member forces from the displacements.

The global matrix is symmetric and usually sparse. Before supports are applied it is singular, because the structure can move as a rigid body.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Take the two-span beam with AB = 6 m, BC = 4 m and a load of 20 kN/m, with pins at A, B and C. Use a modified stiffness for the pinned far ends, so the only unknown is the rotation θ at B.

Stiffness at B: K = 3EI/6 + 3EI/4 = 1.25EI
Load term from fixed end moments: 90 − 40 = 50 kN·m
θ = 50 ÷ 1.25EI = 40 ÷ EI

MBA = 90 − (3EI/6)(40 ÷ EI) = 90 − 20 = 70 kN·m

This matches the moment distribution result. Verify large models with hand checks, such as total load against total reactions.

keyPoints: The stiffness equation is [K]{d} = {F}.
Displacements are the unknowns in the stiffness method.
A joint in a plane frame has three degrees of freedom.
The unsupported global matrix is singular.
Member loads become equivalent joint loads through fixed end forces.
Verify models with hand checks.

en.title: Advanced structural analysis: plastic, non-linear and dynamic behaviour
en.short: Plastic collapse, geometric non-linearity, damping and resonance, and earthquake analysis.

sections.heading: Plastic collapse
sections.text:
Elastic analysis stops at first yield, yet ductile steel beams have further reserve. When a whole section yields, it forms a plastic hinge at the plastic moment Mp = fy S, where S is the plastic modulus. The shape factor S ÷ Z is 1.5 for a rectangle.

An indeterminate structure collapses only after enough hinges form to create a mechanism. The upper bound theorem: any assumed mechanism gives a collapse load at or above the true value. The lower bound theorem: any safe, equilibrium moment pattern gives a load at or below it.

Example: a fixed-ended beam carries a uniform load. Hinges form at both ends and at mid-span, and wc = 16Mp ÷ L². With Mp = 200 kN·m and L = 8 m:
wc = 16 × 200 ÷ 8² = 50 kN/m

sections.heading: Non-linear analysis
sections.text: Linear analysis assumes small displacements and elastic material. Geometric non-linearity arises when deformation changes the forces. The P-Δ effect is an example: a sideways displacement Δ under a vertical load P adds extra moment. Material non-linearity arises from yielding and from cracking of concrete. Non-linear problems are solved in steps, often by Newton-Raphson iteration, and superposition no longer applies.

sections.heading: Structural dynamics
sections.text:
The equation of motion for one degree of freedom is:
mü + cu̇ + ku = F(t)
Damping is expressed as the ratio ζ of the damping to its critical value. For harmonic loads, the dynamic amplification factor is:
D = 1 ÷ √[(1 − β²)² + (2ζβ)²]
where β is the forcing frequency divided by the natural frequency.

Example: β = 0.9 and ζ = 0.05.
D = 1 ÷ √(0.0361 + 0.0081) = 1 ÷ 0.2102 = 4.76

For many degrees of freedom, modal analysis separates the response into natural modes. Earthquake design commonly uses a response spectrum, which gives peak response against natural period. Seismic codes such as Eurocode 8 apply where the local hazard requires them.

keyPoints: A plastic hinge forms at Mp = fy S.
Fixed-ended beam under uniform load: wc = 16Mp ÷ L².
Upper bound methods give loads at or above the true collapse load.
Superposition doesn’t apply to non-linear problems.
Modal analysis separates a structure’s response into natural modes.

en.title: The finite element method
en.short: Elements, shape functions and stiffness, a worked bar model, and how to judge FE results.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text:
The finite element method solves problems that have no simple exact solution, such as slabs with openings, dams and soil-structure interaction. The continuous body is divided into small elements joined at nodes. Within each element, the displacement is approximated from its nodal values:
u(x) = Σ Nᵢ(x) uᵢ
The Nᵢ are shape functions. For a two-node bar of length L, they are N₁ = 1 − x/L and N₂ = x/L.

The element stiffness comes from the strain-displacement matrix [B] and the material matrix [D]:
[k] = ∫ [B]ᵀ[D][B] dV
For the bar, this gives k = (EA ÷ L) × [1, −1; −1, 1].

Isoparametric elements map curved shapes onto a simple reference element, and Gauss quadrature evaluates the integrals numerically.

sections.heading: Worked example: a bar with two elements
sections.text:
A bar is fixed at node 1, with EA = 100,000 kN and total length 2 m. A load of 50 kN acts at free end node 3. Use two elements of 1 m each, so k = EA ÷ L = 100,000 kN/m.

After assembly and removing node 1:
[2k, −k; −k, k]{u₂; u₃} = {0; 50}

From row 1: 2ku₂ − ku₃ = 0, so u₃ = 2u₂.
From row 2: −ku₂ + 2ku₂ = 50, so u₂ = 50 ÷ 100,000 = 0.0005 m = 0.5 mm.
Then u₃ = 1.0 mm.

Check: the exact value is PL ÷ (EA) = 50 × 2 ÷ 100,000 = 0.001 m = 1.0 mm. It is exact here because linear elements represent constant strain exactly.

sections.heading: Judging results

keyPoints: FEM divides a body into elements joined at nodes.
Shape functions interpolate displacement within an element.
Element stiffness is [k] = ∫ [B]ᵀ[D][B] dV.
Run a convergence study by refining the mesh.
Check reactions and compare with a hand calculation or benchmark.
Stress at sharp corners can grow without limit as the mesh is refined.

en.title: Research methods in civil engineering
en.short: Framing a question, choosing methods, analysing data, reporting uncertainty and writing a dissertation.

sections.heading: From question to method
sections.text:
Research starts with a clear question that can be answered within the time and budget. For example: how does replacing 20% of cement with rice husk ash affect the 28-day strength of concrete made with local aggregates in northern Ghana?

A literature review shows what is already known and where the gap lies. Civil engineering research commonly uses laboratory experiments, field monitoring, numerical modelling, surveys of practitioners or case studies. Choose the method that fits the question.

Good experimental design changes one factor at a time, or uses a factorial design to study interactions. It includes control specimens, enough repeats and randomised casting or testing where possible. Calibrate equipment and record it so that others could repeat the work. A numerical model needs validation against test data, and its sensitivity to input values should be studied.

sections.heading: Worked example: analysing test results
sections.text:
Six cubes give strengths in N/mm² of 28.5, 30.2, 29.0, 31.1, 27.8 and 30.4.

Mean = 177.0 ÷ 6 = 29.5
Sum of squared deviations = 8.00
Standard deviation s = √(8.00 ÷ 5) = 1.26
Coefficient of variation = 1.26 ÷ 29.5 = 4.3%

For a 95% confidence interval on the mean, with 5 degrees of freedom, t = 2.571:
Half-width = 2.571 × 1.265 ÷ √6 = 1.33
Interval = 28.2 to 30.8 N/mm²

Report results with their uncertainty. A difference between two mixes matters only if it is large compared with this scatter, and a t-test or analysis of variance can test this. Statistical significance doesn’t by itself mean practical importance.

sections.heading: Writing and integrity
sections.text:
A dissertation usually has an introduction, literature review, methodology, results, discussion, conclusions and references. Keep results and interpretation clearly apart. State the limits of your work, and don’t claim more than the data supports.

Cite all sources and write in your own words, as plagiarism is a serious offence. Never invent or selectively remove data. Get ethics approval for surveys and interviews where your institution requires it.

keyPoints: Start with a clear question that can be answered within the time and budget.
Include control specimens and enough repeats.
Validate numerical models against test data.
Report results with uncertainty, such as a confidence interval.
Statistical significance doesn’t by itself mean practical importance.
Never invent data, and cite all sources.
